note: Optional, low-burden activity suggestions. Nothing here is a treatment prescription. A recommendation is only offered when a rule explicitly asks for it.

recommendations.title: A short walk, no pressure
recommendations.summary: Ten minutes outside or around your room, at whatever pace feels possible.
recommendations.why: Gentle movement can shift attention and give the day a small, completed shape.
steps: Choose a distance that feels almost too easy.
Set a timer for 10 minutes (or 5 if 10 feels like too much).
Notice one thing you can see, hear and feel.
Stop when the timer ends. That counts.

recommendations.title: Five-minute brain dump
recommendations.summary: Write whatever is in your head for five minutes, without editing it.
recommendations.why: Putting a feeling into words can make it feel less tangled and more approachable.
steps: Open a notes app or take a piece of paper.
Write for five minutes without correcting spelling or grammar.
Finish with one sentence: 'Right now, the main thing is...'
You never have to show it to anyone.
recommendations.caution: If writing about a difficult memory feels overwhelming, stop and do something grounding instead.

recommendations.title: Box breathing
recommendations.summary: A slow four-part breath: in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4.
recommendations.why: Slowing the breath gives your body a clear, simple signal that it can settle.
steps: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop.
Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts.
Hold gently for 4, then breathe out for 4.
Hold for 4, then repeat up to 6 rounds.
If holding feels uncomfortable, skip the holds and just breathe out slowly.
recommendations.caution: Stop if you feel dizzy. Never force a breath.

recommendations.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
recommendations.summary: Anchor your attention in the room using your five senses.
recommendations.why: When thoughts are racing, sensory details give attention somewhere concrete to land.
steps: Name 5 things you can see.
Name 4 things you can touch.
Name 3 things you can hear.
Name 2 things you can smell (or two smells you like).
Name 1 thing you can taste, or take one slow sip of water.

habit_template.name: Use a grounding exercise when needed

recommendations.title: Build a small wind-down
recommendations.summary: Pick three quiet steps to repeat before bed, starting 30 minutes earlier.
recommendations.why: A predictable wind-down helps the brain recognise that the day is ending.
steps: Choose a realistic bedtime you can repeat most nights.
Dim the lights and put screens out of reach 20–30 minutes before bed.
Do the same two or three calm things each night: wash up, stretch, read, or listen to something quiet.
If sleep does not come, rest in dim light rather than forcing it.
Keep the same wake-up time where you can.
recommendations.caution: If sleep problems last for weeks, or you snore heavily or feel sleepy while driving, speak to a doctor.

recommendations.title: One glass of water
recommendations.summary: A single glass now, not a perfect hydration plan.
recommendations.why: Small physical care steps are easy to complete and can interrupt a long stretch of neglect.
steps: Fill a glass or bottle.
Drink it slowly where you are sitting.
Refill it and keep it visible for later.

recommendations.title: Send one low-pressure message
recommendations.summary: A short text to someone safe — no long explanation required.
recommendations.why: Connection does not have to be a big conversation. A small signal can reduce the sense of being alone with things.
steps: Choose one person who tends to be kind.
Send: 'Hey, thinking of you. How are you?' or 'Hi, I'm having a rough day. Can we chat for a bit?'
You do not owe anyone a full update.
If nobody comes to mind, think of a helpline as a real conversation option.

recommendations.title: A real ten-minute break
recommendations.summary: Step away from the task, not just from one tab.
recommendations.why: Rest is part of effort, not a reward you have to earn.
steps: Set a timer for 10 minutes.
Stand up and move away from your desk or study spot.
Choose something low-demand: water, stretching, looking outside, music.
Return only when the timer ends — or take longer if you need it.

recommendations.title: Three small good things
recommendations.summary: Name three ordinary things that were okay today. They can be tiny.
recommendations.why: This is not about forced positivity; it is about noticing what else is present alongside difficulty.
steps: Write three things that were neutral or pleasant.
They can be as small as a warm cup or a song.
If nothing comes, write 'I got through today' and leave it there.
recommendations.caution: If this feels invalidating, skip it. It is optional.

recommendations.title: Two-minute body scan
recommendations.summary: Move attention slowly from your feet to your face, noticing without fixing.
recommendations.why: Turning attention toward bodily sensation can interrupt a loop of anxious thinking.
steps: Sit or lie down somewhere comfortable.
Bring attention to your feet for a few breaths.
Move slowly upward: legs, belly, hands, shoulders, jaw.
Where you find tightness, breathe out a little longer. No need to change it.

recommendations.title: Read ten pages or ten minutes
recommendations.summary: Something gentle and absorbing, not something that feels like homework.
recommendations.why: A contained, low-stakes activity can create a break from rumination.
steps: Pick something you can put down easily.
Read for ten minutes with a timer.
If your attention drifts, that is not failure. Return to the page or stop.

recommendations.title: Five minutes of daylight
recommendations.summary: Open a curtain or step outside for a few minutes of natural light.
recommendations.why: Daylight and a change of scene can support your body clock and break up a long indoor stretch.
steps: Open the curtains or step near a window.
Stay for five minutes without needing to do anything productive.
If you can go outside, notice the air and the temperature.
recommendations.caution: Use sun protection if you stay out longer.

recommendations.title: Reset one small area
recommendations.summary: Clear one surface, make the bed, or put away five things. Not the whole room.
recommendations.why: A visible, bounded change can create a small sense of agency on an overwhelming day.
steps: Choose one surface or one small category of objects.
Set a five-minute timer.
Stop when the timer ends, even if it is not perfect.

recommendations.title: One song with full attention
recommendations.summary: Listen to a song you like without doing anything else.
recommendations.why: Music can give a feeling somewhere to go when words are hard.
steps: Choose one song — calming or cathartic, whichever fits.
Pause other tasks and listen to the whole thing.
Notice what changes in your body or mood, with no judgement.

habit_template.name: Listen to one song with full attention

recommendations.title: A gentle stretch
recommendations.summary: Unclench your jaw, roll your shoulders, stretch your neck and back.
recommendations.why: Stress often settles in the body; a slow stretch can release some of that physical holding.
steps: Sit or stand comfortably.
Roll your shoulders back three times.
Tilt your head slowly side to side.
Reach your arms overhead and breathe out.
Stop anywhere that hurts.
recommendations.caution: Do not push into pain. Check with a doctor if you have an injury.

recommendations.title: Choose just one next thing
recommendations.summary: When everything feels urgent, reduce the list to one task and one first step.
recommendations.why: Overwhelm shrinks when the next action is specific, small and time-bound.
steps: Write down everything on your mind for two minutes.
Circle the one thing that matters most today.
Under it, write the smallest physical first step (open the file, find the page, send the message).
Set a 10-minute timer and do only that step.

recommendations.title: One 25-minute focus block
recommendations.summary: A single timed block with a clear, narrow goal — then a real break.
recommendations.why: A short, bounded study block is easier to start than an open-ended plan.
steps: Choose one small outcome for the block.
Put your phone out of reach and set a 25-minute timer.
Work only on that outcome.
Take a 5-minute break afterwards, whether or not it went perfectly.
recommendations.caution: If you are exhausted, a break is a better choice than pushing through.

recommendations.title: A contained worry window
recommendations.summary: Set aside 10 minutes to write worries down, then close the notebook.
recommendations.why: Containing worry to a specific time can reduce how much it spills into the whole day.
steps: Set a 10-minute timer.
Write each worry as a sentence.
Mark each one: 'can act on it' or 'not in my control right now'.
Choose one small action for one actionable worry.
Close the notebook when the timer ends.
recommendations.caution: If this becomes a rumination session, stop and use a grounding exercise.

recommendations.title: Rewrite one harsh sentence
recommendations.summary: Take one self-critical thought and write what you would say to a friend in the same situation.
recommendations.why: Changing the tone of an inner sentence can loosen its grip, even when the situation has not changed.
steps: Write the harsh thought exactly as it appears.
Ask: would I say this to a friend I care about?
Write a fairer version that is still honest — not fake positivity.
Read the fairer version out loud once.

recommendations.title: One small screen boundary
recommendations.summary: Move one app off the home screen, or set a single timer for scrolling.
recommendations.why: A small environmental change is often easier than relying on willpower alone.
steps: Choose one app that tends to swallow time.
Move it off the home screen or set a 20-minute timer.
Put a book, water or something else within reach.
Notice the urge without needing to obey it.

recommendations.title: The 90-second pause
recommendations.summary: Before responding, step away and let the first wave of anger move through your body.
recommendations.why: A short pause creates space between a strong feeling and an action you might regret.
steps: Name it silently: 'This is anger.'
Put both feet on the floor and unclench your hands.
Breathe out longer than you breathe in for five breaths.
If possible, leave the room for two minutes.
Decide what to do only after the pause.
recommendations.caution: If you feel you might hurt someone, move away and contact someone you trust or emergency services.

recommendations.title: A small remembering ritual
recommendations.summary: Do one small thing that honours the person or loss — a photo, a song, a letter, a memory.
recommendations.why: Grief does not need to be rushed or fixed. A ritual can give it a gentle place.
steps: Choose one memory or object that feels manageable today.
Spend five minutes with it: look at a photo, listen to a song, write a short note.
Say or write one thing you want to remember.
Close by doing something soothing — water, fresh air, a warm drink.
recommendations.caution: If grief feels unsafe or you are not able to function day to day, please reach out to a professional.

recommendations.title: One small social step
recommendations.summary: Choose the smallest social contact that feels slightly possible — a nod, a message, a short hello.
recommendations.why: Avoiding social situations reduces anxiety in the short term but can make it grow. Tiny steps build evidence that you can cope.
steps: Pick a low-stakes situation: message one person, greet a classmate, ask a shop assistant a question.
Set a tiny goal: 10 seconds of contact is enough.
Notice any anxiety without waiting for it to disappear first.
Write down what actually happened, not what you feared.
recommendations.caution: This is a self-help idea, not a therapy protocol. A therapist can help design graded steps.

recommendations.title: Consider talking to a professional
recommendations.summary: A counsellor, doctor or mental health professional can offer assessment and options that this app cannot.
recommendations.why: Persistent or severe difficulties deserve a real clinical conversation — not because you have failed at self-help.
steps: Note two or three things you want help with.
Consider a college counsellor, a family doctor, or a licensed therapist.
Ask someone you trust to help you make the first call if that makes it easier.
In India you can also call Tele-MANAS on 14416 to ask how to access care.
recommendations.caution: This app cannot diagnose or treat any condition.

recommendations.title: Make a simple safety plan
recommendations.summary: A short plan for the next hour: who to contact, where to go, what to remove from reach.
recommendations.why: When things feel unsafe, a concrete plan reduces the number of decisions you have to make in a crisis.
steps: Tell one trusted person how you are feeling right now.
Move away from anything you could use to hurt yourself, and ask someone to hold it.
Go to a place with another person, or call a helpline and stay on the line.
Call 112 if you are in immediate danger. Call Tele-MANAS 14416 for mental health support.
Write down the number of one person you will contact if things get worse.
recommendations.caution: This plan does not replace emergency services. If you are in immediate danger, call 112 now.

recommendations.title: Reconnect with what matters
recommendations.summary: Name one value you want to act on today, and one tiny action that fits it.
recommendations.why: When mood is low, values can offer direction when motivation is not available.
steps: Pick one word: kindness, honesty, connection, curiosity, care, courage.
Ask: what would one small action in that direction look like today?
Do the smallest version within the next hour.
Notice the action, not the outcome.
